title: Owning It vs. Being Stuck With It

conversation.headline: Owning It vs. Being Stuck With It
paragraphs: I was talking with Alex Judd about weaknesses, and he laid out three ways people deal with them: pretend they don't exist, admit they exist but assume you can't change, or own it — build the skill, delegate it, or hire for it.
I'd put myself in camp three for most of my life. Not this one.

We had an employee who wasn't meeting our standards. A client complained to me directly. Instead of bringing it to my partner — who runs operations, not me — as his call to make, I came in hot: "This guy has to go." My partner never even heard the real complaint, because of how I delivered it. It took an extra three weeks to sort out, and we nearly lost a great client over it.

Looking back, the honest answer isn't that I was rushing to protect the client relationship. It was that I was speaking from "this is my truth" — and treating that as the same thing as correct. Truth and effectiveness aren't the same thing.

I'm not at stage three here. I'm at maybe 2.5 — working on the skill of delivering truth only when it's actually useful, not just when it's accurate. These days, when a complaint comes in, I don't call immediately. I sit with it first and ask what an effective approach looks like, instead of reacting.
▶ Full episode with Alex Judd | ▶ Short: Owning Your Weaknesses vs. Denying They Exist
conversation.takeaway: Next time you're certain you're right about something, pause before you say it and ask: is this the true thing, or the useful thing? If you're not sure, that's your sign to wait.

build.headline: Revamping the Brand — the Honest Version
paragraphs: We just went through a full brand revamp at Better Ledgers, and I want to be straight about why now: AI finally made it easy.

When we first did our branding, the visuals were great. The voice, mission, and core values underneath them weren't — none of it was based on anything concrete. We hadn't nailed down our role in the market or what made us different from every other bookkeeping firm. Our old tagline was "Trusted Partners, Seamless Solutions." I'll let you try to figure out what that actually means. I couldn't, and I wrote it.

Here's what changed: I've learned that when I need clarity, what I actually need isn't a blank page — it's someone asking me the right questions until the answer falls out. So I had AI interview me. Real questions: how do we actually operate, what's true about our old branding and what isn't, why do we exist in plain English. I told it stories — how we've actually treated customers, what we've done when things went wrong. It gave me a draft back. Then I went through it line by line and rewrote it into our actual voice, not AI's version of our voice.

What came out of it: our new tagline is "Built for Business." It says the thing the old one didn't — we operate on a business's timeline. Books updated daily, so reports are always ready when you need them, not weeks behind. Our mission and values got the same treatment: rebuilt to reflect how we actually run things, not how a branding template said a bookkeeping firm should sound.
build.takeaway: If your brand, plan, or pitch feels vague, the fix probably isn't a better writer — it's better questions. Find something, or someone, that will interrogate your "why" until you can say it in plain English.

thinking.headline: As Long As It's a Theory, It Stays Scary
paragraphs: A friend told me he's thinking about starting a private social media channel to grow his business. Listening to him, it was obvious — he wants to do it. Something else was doing the talking: the excuses.

I've been there twice. It took me eight months of going back and forth before I started my podcast, until I realized I was going to suck at first no matter what, and the sooner I started, the sooner that would stop being true. Same thing when I was working through my eating disorder — the longer I avoided a food or a situation, the bigger the anxiety got.
As long as something lives in your head, it'll always be scary.

Doesn't matter if it's starting a business, flying a plane, bungee jumping, or starting a new job. The fear isn't really about the risk — it's about the not-knowing that comes from never acting. Once you're actually in it, you know how to handle what comes up. Before that, your brain will invent problems just to justify staying still.

Easy to say to a friend. Harder to sit with when I turn it on myself — because right now, I'm doing the exact same thing. A few newsletters back I mentioned wanting to build a new content strategy for Better Ledgers. Since then: nothing. Not because I don't have time, but because I keep waiting for the "right" version of the plan before I start. Which is its own excuse — trying to make it perfect is just a slower way of avoiding it.
thinking.takeaway: Pick the one thing you've been "thinking about" instead of doing. Take the smallest real action on it today — even a bad one — and notice how much the anxiety drops the second it stops being a theory.
